title: Nepal, South Korea seal landmark climate deal - The Rising Nepal
description: Nepal, South Korea seal landmark climate deal  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
By A Staff Reporter

Kathmandu, Nov. 14: The Government of Nepal and the Government of the Republic of Korea have signed a landmark Framework Agreement for Cooperation on Climate Change, marking a significant milestone in strengthening bilateral cooperation on carbon finance, greenhouse gas emission reductions, climate resilience and sustainable development.

The Agreement establishes a comprehensive framework for cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, creating new opportunities to mobilize international carbon finance, promote climate-friendly investments, facilitate technology transfer, and support both countries in achieving their Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs), according to a press statement issued by Ministry of Agriculture, Forest and Environment on Friday.

For Nepal, one of the world's most climate-vulnerable mountainous countries, this partnership represents an important step towards unlocking innovative climate finance and accelerating its transition towards a low-carbon, climate-resilient economy, it said.

A central feature of the Agreement is the promotion of voluntary cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, enabling the development of carbon mitigation projects and the potential transfer of internationally recognized mitigation outcomes between the two countries.

According to the statement, the partnership will encourage public and private sector investments in priority sectors, including renewable energy, transportation, industry, buildings, waste management, agriculture, and forestry.

The Agreement also provides for transparent carbon accounting, monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV), corresponding adjustments, and safeguards against double counting, ensuring environmental integrity and compliance with international climate commitments. Beyond carbon markets, the Agreement promotes cooperation in climate science, research, technological innovation, adaptation, methane reduction, and just energy transition.

It will facilitate exchanges among government institutions, researchers, universities, investors, and private sector organizations, strengthening Nepal's technical and institutional capacity to implement ambitious climate actions. The partnership is particularly relevant to Nepal's climate priorities, including implementation of its NDC 3.0, strengthening climate resilience, and pursuing its long-term objective of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2045.

The Agreement provides for the establishment of a Joint Committee on Climate Change Cooperation, comprising representatives of both governments, to coordinate implementation, approve joint work plans, and oversee cooperative activities.

The Committee may establish specialized subcommittees on carbon market mechanisms and climate science and technology to facilitate effective implementation. The Government of Nepal welcomes this important partnership with the Republic of Korea as a demonstration of international solidarity and shared responsibility in addressing climate change.

At a time when Nepal is experiencing increasingly severe climate-related disasters, including catastrophic floods and growing risks across the Himalayan region, innovative financing partnerships are essential to support sustainable development and strengthen national resilience.

Nepal looks forward to translating this Agreement into concrete investments, technology partnerships, capacity-building initiatives, and measurable climate outcomes that benefit both countries. The Government of Nepal has expressed its sincere appreciation to the Government of the Republic of Korea for its partnership and commitment to advancing effective, transparent, and mutually beneficial climate cooperation.

title: Cyber scam response centre launched - The Rising Nepal
description: Cyber scam response centre launched  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
Kathmandu, Nov. 14: The Integrated Anti-Cyber Scam Centre (IACSC) has come into operation with the objective of curbing the growing incidents of cyber scams and digital financial fraud.

The Centre formally began providing services from November 6. As soon as the new Police Chief Dr. Manoj KC assumed the post, the service which had been stalled for last few months began its service being based at a newly built Cyber Bureau Office in Samakhusi, Kathmandu.

It was established in accordance with the Guidelines on the Establishment and Operation of the Integrated Anti-Cyber Scam Centre, 2083, approved by a ministerial-level decision of the Government of Nepal on October 9, 2026.

The Centre has brought together representatives from regulatory bodies, Nepal Police, banks and financial institutions, digital wallet service providers, telecommunications companies and internet service providers. They will work in coordination from a common physical facility to ensure a prompt response to cyber scams and digital financial fraud, said Deputy Inspector General and Central Spokesperson for the Police Headquarters, Abi Narayan Kafle.

The initiative aims to minimise potential financial losses and risks by ensuring immediate and effective responses to incidents of cyber fraud. It also seeks to make Nepal's digital financial system safer, more reliable and trustworthy, he added.

A designated contact officer has been assigned to receive complaints and information related to cyber fraud round the clock. The Centre has also introduced an emergency hotline, 1247, for reporting such incidents.

Through direct coordination and information-sharing among the concerned agencies, the Centre is expected to facilitate the identification of individuals involved in fraudulent activities, the timely detection of suspicious transactions and efforts to secure victims' funds, said DIG Kafle.

As the use of digital payments and online transactions continues to expand in the country, cyber fraud has emerged as an increasingly serious challenge. The operation of the integrated response centre is therefore being viewed as a significant step towards strengthening the country's digital financial security, added DIG Kafle.

The Centre, led by the Ministry of Home Affairs and Nepal Police, has been providing round-the-clock services since November 6, 2026. People who fall victim to digital fraud or suspect suspicious activity involving their financial transactions can immediately call the emergency hotline 1247 to seek assistance for securing their money, said DIG Nabindra Aryal, Chief of the Cyber Bureau.

Its establishment follows growing concerns over the financial losses caused by online fraud and the difficulties victims face in recovering stolen money because of delays in coordination among law enforcement agencies, banks and payment service providers, said Aryal.

According to the Bureau, the Centre is designed to enable authorities to trace suspicious transactions, identify beneficiary accounts and coordinate with banks and wallet operators to freeze funds before scammers can withdraw or transfer them. Under the prescribed response mechanism, complaints are to be registered and classified within 10 minutes, while requests to freeze suspicious accounts and funds are expected to be initiated within 10 to 60 minutes.

The need for such a mechanism has become increasingly urgent, with police receiving between 200 and 300 cyber-fraud complaints daily, according to figures cited by the Cyber Bureau before the centre was established.

Only around 10 per cent of the money lost to online scams was being recovered under the previous system, highlighting the difficulties caused by delays in coordination and fund-tracing procedures, said DIG Aryal.

The new mechanism has already shown promising results. Nepal Rastra Bank Director Sushil Paudel said the centre had successfully stopped fraudulent transactions across as many as nine layers of bank accounts within 15 minutes. Representatives of 20 banks, along with digital wallet operators Khalti and eSewa, were stationed at the Centre, according to him.

The centre had also been receiving an average of three complaints an hour shortly after beginning operations, informed Aryal.

The Centre is expected to strengthen cooperation between the public and private sectors by bringing financial institutions, law enforcement agencies and telecommunications service providers into a common response mechanism.

Its broader responsibilities include tracing the movement of stolen money, identifying suspicious accounts and wallets, and taking action against mobile numbers, SIM cards, phishing websites and other digital platforms used in fraudulent activities, stated the Bureau.

title: Nepal demands grants, not loans, to finance climate action at COP31 - myRepublica
description: Nepal demands grants, not loans, to finance climate action at COP31  myRepublica
publisher.title: myRepublica
full_article:
ANTALYA, November 14: Nepal has called on developed countries and international financial institutions to provide climate finance primarily in the form of grants rather than loans, arguing that countries least responsible for global greenhouse gas emissions should not be pushed into further debt to cope with the impacts of climate change.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

The call was made during a high-level side event at the Nepal Pavilion at the ongoing UN Climate Change Conference (COP31) in Antalya, where participants highlighted the growing gap between international climate finance commitments and the resources actually reaching vulnerable communities.

The discussion, titled “Unpacking Climate Finance in Nepal: Access, Quality and Equity”, was organized by the NGO Federation of Nepal (NFN) in collaboration with Oxfam. Speakers stressed that climate finance must be adequate, predictable, transparent and accessible, with priority given to grants for adaptation and addressing loss and damage.

Figures presented during the discussion showed that Nepal received around $5.71 billion in international climate finance between 2011 and 2021. However, 61 percent of the financing was in the form of loans, 38 percent as grants and the remaining one percent as equity and other investments.

The figures have renewed concerns over the growing debt burden on climate-vulnerable countries that have contributed relatively little to the climate crisis but are increasingly exposed to its devastating consequences.

Related story SHIFT for Our Planet: Youths urge authorities to make climate j...

“Climate finance is not just about money; it is about justice, dignity, and survival. Nepal contributes very little to global greenhouse gas emissions, yet our communities are suffering the devastating impacts of climate change. We need grants, not loans; action, not promises; and climate justice, not charity,” said Arjun Bhattarai, president of the NGO Federation of Nepal.

The discussion brought together Arjun Dhakal, undersecretary and climate change focal person at the Government of Nepal; Neha Sharma, representing the Adaptation Fund; Dr Manish Raj Pandey, director of the National Trust for Nature Conservation (NTNC); and climate activist Harjeet Singh.

Dhakal said the choice between grants and loans should depend on the nature of projects, their requirements, the availability of financial resources and potential economic returns. He argued that grants should be prioritized for adaptation projects, many of which do not generate direct financial returns.

However, concessional loans could be considered for renewable energy, hydropower and climate-related infrastructure projects capable of generating economic benefits, he said. He also stressed the need to assess repayment periods, grace periods and the country's overall debt sustainability before accepting external loans.

Sharma highlighted the importance of strengthening national institutions to improve their direct access to international climate funds. She said institutions seeking accreditation must meet requirements related to gender equality, environmental and social safeguards, procurement and financial management.

She also highlighted the Adaptation Fund's readiness support programme, which helps national institutions build their capacity to develop and implement climate projects.

Pandey shared Nepal's experience in biodiversity conservation, access to genetic resources and benefit-sharing arrangements, highlighting the importance of institutional and legal frameworks in ensuring the equitable distribution of benefits.

Climate activist Singh argued that climate finance should be treated as an obligation of countries historically responsible for greenhouse gas emissions rather than as charity or development assistance. He criticized developed countries for failing to provide adequate resources while continuing to spend heavily on fossil fuel industries and other sectors.

He also said vulnerable countries should not have to borrow money to protect themselves from climate impacts they did little to cause, calling for greater funding for both adaptation and loss and damage.

Meanwhile, a separate high-level programme at the Nepal Pavilion focused on translating climate finance commitments into large-scale adaptation action. The programme, titled “From Climate Finance Commitments to Adaptation at Scale”, was co-hosted by the Government of Nepal and the Asian Development Bank (ADB). At the event, Sumnima Udas highlighted the Green and Resilience Financing Facility (GREFF) as a country-led platform to connect Nepal's adaptation priorities with international climate finance.

Udas stressed that international support works best when aligned with national adaptation priorities and delivered through the country's own systems. She said climate finance commitments must be translated into investment-ready adaptation programmes that deliver tangible benefits to vulnerable people. She also noted that Nepal's experience could offer lessons for other climate-vulnerable countries across the Hindu Kush Himalaya and beyond.

The NGO Federation called on governments, international financial institutions and climate finance mechanisms to improve direct access to funding and ensure the meaningful participation of civil society organizations, local governments and affected communities in climate-related decision-making.

title: PM asks lawmakers to advance Nepal’s interest in China ties - The Kathmandu Post
description: PM asks lawmakers to advance Nepal’s interest in China ties  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s diplomatic engagement with its two powerful neighbours is gathering momentum, with Prime Minister Balendra Shah preparing to visit India while a 20-member delegation of lawmakers from his party heads to China, in a move that underscores Kathmandu’s effort to maintain a balance in its foreign relations.

The parallel engagements come at a politically significant moment for Shah, who is preparing for his first official bilateral visit abroad since assuming office in March. While he is scheduled to travel to New Delhi on November 22, a high-level delegation of the ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party (RSP) is leaving for Beijing on Sunday for nearly two weeks of political and diplomatic engagement.

The timing of the two visits has drawn attention to Nepal’s traditional geopolitical challenge: maintaining close relations with India and China without becoming entangled in their competing strategic interests.

Before their departure, Shah met the lawmakers at Singha Durbar on Friday and urged them to put Nepal’s national interests at the centre of their discussions with Chinese officials.

The delegation, led by RSP general secretary and lawmaker Bipin Acharya, was advised to discuss the Belt and Road Initiative (BRI), Chinese-funded projects, tourism, economic cooperation, and the implementation of past bilateral agreements.

Although the visit is being undertaken by ruling party lawmakers rather than an official government delegation, Shah made it clear that they would be representing the ruling party and, by extension, the country's political establishment.

“Although you are not part of the government, you represent the ruling party, so you should feel free to raise the issues that matter to Nepal,” a lawmaker who attended the meeting quoted Shah as saying.

The prime minister also urged the lawmakers not to approach China with an inferiority complex because Nepal is a smaller country.

The message reflects the new government's attempt to engage both neighbours from a position of confidence while avoiding the perception that Kathmandu is tilting towards either side.

In particular, Shah asked the delegation to examine how Nepal could benefit from the BRI, an initiative that has remained contentious in Nepal because of concerns over financing, implementation and the country's ability to manage debt.

“There has been considerable debate and controversy surrounding the BRI, so you need to approach the subject carefully. Make it clear how Nepal can use the initiative in its national interest,” another lawmaker quoted Shah as saying.

He also suggested raising the possibility of converting Chinese loans extended for airport projects into grants, although he acknowledged that the delegation was unlikely to secure such a commitment during the visit.

The discussion comes as Nepal seeks to resolve questions surrounding Chinese-funded infrastructure projects, including those that have made little progress despite bilateral agreements.

Shah asked the lawmakers to seek clarity from Chinese officials about stalled projects and what needs to be done to advance their implementation.

The delegation will also explore opportunities for cooperation under China's Global Development Initiative, particularly in tourism, infrastructure and economic development.

In Beijing, the lawmakers are scheduled to meet a member of the Chinese Communist Party's Politburo and senior officials from the party's International Department. The Chinese Communist Party asked the RSP to send a high-level delegation and is arranging the visit.

Deputy parliamentary party leader Ganesh Parajuli said the prime minister had also emphasised the importance of maintaining Nepal's non-aligned foreign policy.

“He advised us on how to raise the commitments made by the state and the progress of bilateral agreements while safeguarding Nepal’s non-aligned foreign policy. He also stressed that Nepal should maintain balanced relations with both its neighbours and other countries,” Parajuli said.

Meanwhile, Shah's planned visit to India carries considerable economic and diplomatic significance.

His decision to travel to New Delhi marks a departure from his earlier position of not undertaking foreign visits during his first year in office. He responded positively to an invitation from Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, conveyed by Indian Foreign Secretary Vikram Misri during his November 4-5 visit to Kathmandu.

The two sides discussed a range of bilateral issues, including Nepal's proposal for a $2 billion economic assistance package from India.

Kathmandu has sought $1 billion in grants and another $1 billion in concessional loans to finance infrastructure and development projects. The proposed grants include $500 million for the Butwal-Pokhara Expressway and another $500 million for reconstructing infrastructure damaged by the Bhotekoshi flash flood.

The proposed loans would primarily finance hydropower projects and electricity transmission lines. Nepal has also requested that the loans be provided in Indian rupees rather than US dollars to reduce foreign exchange risks.

Other issues on the bilateral agenda include the Pancheshwar Multipurpose Project, petroleum pipelines connecting India and Nepal, trade, energy cooperation, and connectivity.

Kathmandu has also proposed establishing branches of India's prestigious Indian Institutes of Technology and Indian Institutes of Management in Nepal, alongside cooperation in artificial intelligence and technical assistance for cricket development.

However, former foreign secretary Madhu Raman Acharya has cautioned the government against approaching the India visit with an extensive wish list.

“Ask no favour and take no wish list along. Talk to the other side eye to eye as an equal counterpart,” Acharya told the Post, the sister publication of Kantipur, in a recent interview .

He said Shah should focus on restoring political trust and confidence with India and resolving issues that require intervention at the highest political level, rather than attempting to settle every bilateral issue during one visit.

“Concentrate on issues that need to be resolved at the highest political level. Focus on building trust and confidence. Let the mechanisms work on the issues; the rest will follow,” he said.

The advice highlights the diplomatic tightrope facing the new government. While Nepal needs India's cooperation in trade, energy, infrastructure and transit, it also seeks Chinese investment and development assistance without compromising its strategic independence.

The parallel engagements with Beijing and New Delhi therefore offer an early indication of how the Shah government intends to manage Nepal's relations with its two neighbours.

RSP chief whip Kabindra Burlakoti said the Beijing visit should go beyond tourism and contribute to the development interests of both countries.

The delegation will not discuss the Nepal-India-China border disputes, as those issues fall within the responsibility of the government and official diplomatic mechanisms, he said.

title: Whispers Of Mountains - The Rising Nepal
description: Whispers Of Mountains  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
BIBEK SHRESTHA

I sometimes imagine a different 29 May 1953. Tenzing Norgay and Edmund Hillary have just stood on the summit of Sagarmatha. But instead of inspiring the world to follow in their footsteps, they turn towards the valley below and say: "This was enough. Please do not climb again."

Before Tenzing joined the expedition, the story goes, his father warned him that Chomolungma would not like it. She was their mother, and one should never walk on one's mother. But history took a different turn. Himalayan communities have understood this for generations. Khumbila is revered as the guardian deity of Khumbu.

These mountains are our water towers, feeding rivers on which more than three billion people depend. So I keep asking: who would step on their own mother? Who would contaminate their own source of freshwater?

Mountaineering in Nepal is relatively young. In 1950, French climbers Maurice Herzog and Louis Lachenal reached the summit of Annapurna I. Three years later, Everest followed. Tourism grew after King Mahendra's coronation in 1955, and Jimmy Roberts later founded Mountain Travel Nepal, the country's first trekking company. An extraordinary pursuit gradually became an industry.

After the Second World War, much of the Western world entered an era of growing prosperity and material consumption. People chased money and comfort. I sometimes wonder whether adventure tourism became an escape from that restlessness: another experience to purchase in a world where almost everything had acquired a price tag.

Better climbing gear, satellite weather forecasts, roads into remote valleys and the fascination with summit photographs changed mountaineering. Climbing became more accessible and commercial. By June 2026, more than 7,500 people had stood on Everest, making over 15,700 ascents.

Figures attributed to Nepal's Ministry of Culture and Tourism estimate that Everest holds around 150 tonnes of waste, with another 12 tonnes added each season. Kanchenjunga and Annapurna I are also reported to carry about 12 tonnes each. We leave behind empty oxygen cylinders, torn tents, ropes, crampons, batteries, syringes, gas canisters and human excrement. Microplastics have also been detected in Everest's snow.

An average climber reportedly generates 18 to 25 kilograms of waste per expedition. The government introduced a US$4,000 deposit, refundable when climbers bring their rubbish back, but experts say the system has failed. Climbers often bring down what is easier to collect from lower camps, while rubbish at higher camps remains behind.

Waste does not disappear simply because we stop seeing it. At higher camps, human excrement is often buried in shallow holes or left exposed. It can seep into snow and glacial water. ICIMOD studies have reported coliform bacteria, including E. coli, in water sources near popular trekking routes and settlements. Those who suffer are not only visitors, but also communities living downstream, whose lives depend on these rivers.

Then there is the firewood burned for trekking groups, the black carbon that accelerates glacial melting and forests thinning near the tree line. We are wearing down a mother we claim to love, one expedition at a time.

Forget about other peaks; more than 200 bodies are believed to remain on Everest alone; recovering them is often too dangerous. Everyone belonged to someone's son, daughter, parent, friend, or beloved. Some lie along popular routes, passed by climbers heading for a summit photograph.

Think about that. A place where generations sought spiritual refuge has become a place where we step over the dead and keep moving towards our own moment of glory. Is that bravery?

I struggle to comprehend our urge to conquer everything within sight. Is it intelligence or simply another expression of human stupidity? They existed long before our ambitions and egos. They nurture ecosystems in which we, with other species, simply exist.

Yet we chase records to become the first, the youngest, the fastest, or the hundredth. These records mean nothing to the mountains and little to anyone but the climber. Behind this ego stands money. Permits, expedition packages, oxygen cylinders, fixed ropes and guided summits are sold to anyone who can afford to say they stood on top of the world. Ego and money drive these crowds. Neither needs a mountain.

To me, bravery means putting yourself in harm's way to protect others. By that measure, what does modern mountaineering protect? Who is protected when glaciers melt, rivers become polluted and snow leopards lose their habitats to expanding trails and yet another teahouse?

With global temperatures exceeding 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels for the calendar year 2024, it is time to put aside our self-destructive arrogance and restore the balance. We must rethink adventure and whether every mountain needs to be climbed simply because it is there.

The mountains do not need us to conquer them. Perhaps bravery now means standing at the foot of our treasures, silently thanking them for all they have given us.

After all, the most valuable treasures in this world are not jewels or gold. They are the very snow that crowns our mother.

title: Nepal’s high-value exports rise 23.85 percent in first quarter - The Kathmandu Post
description: Nepal’s high-value exports rise 23.85 percent in first quarter  The Kathmandu Post
publisher.title: The Kathmandu Post
full_article:
Nepal’s exports of high-value products rose by 23.85 percent in the first three months of the current fiscal year compared to the same period last fiscal year, driven by higher shipments of large cardamom, iron and steel products, jute and jute products, readymade garments, pashmina shawls, carpets, and felt products.

Exports of products listed under the Nepal Trade Integration Strategy (NTIS) 2023 reached Rs36.65 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year, up from Rs29.59 billion during the same period last fiscal year.

During the review period, Nepal’s overall exports grew by 57.03 percent to Rs114.28 billion, mainly due to the re-export of edible oils, including palm, soyabean, and sunflower oil. The country exported edible oils worth Rs58.42 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year.

Trade experts said exports could have grown further if Nepal had been able to process and package its agricultural products to meet international standards and sell them in different markets.

“The prices of goods have increased globally in recent times, and the dollar has also strengthened, contributing to the rise in exports. Producers might also have been trying to diversify markets beyond India, which could have added to the growth,” said Rabi Shankar Sainju, a trade expert.

Sainju said exports could have registered substantial growth if Nepal had been able to export processed and packaged agricultural products such as large cardamom, ginger, dog chews, and medicinal herbs, among others.

“Our major strategy should be market diversity and product diversity,” he said.

Among the NTIS-listed products, exports of large cardamom, dog chews, fabrics, footwear, ginger, iron and steel products, jute and jute products, Nepali handmade paper, readymade garments, rosin, tea, pashmina, carpets, felt products, yarn, vegetables, spices, coffee, pasta, honey, and gold and silver jewellery increased during the review period.

Exports of large cardamom jumped by 53.19 percent to Rs2.57 billion during the review period, with 1,449 tonnes shipped.

Tighter global supplies, relatively stable prices and sustained demand from South Asian and Middle Eastern markets have pushed the value of Nepal’s large cardamom exports to an all-time high.

Unlike in previous years, prices remained unusually stable this year at around Rs2,500 per kg, encouraging farmers to sell their produce rather than hold stocks in anticipation of further price increases.

India remains the dominant buyer, accounting for around 99 percent of Nepal’s large cardamom exports. The spice is then re-exported from India to Pakistan and countries in the Middle East, where Nepali cardamom commands premium prices because of its distinctive flavour and quality.

The country exported 6,395 tonnes of large cardamom worth Rs12.64 billion in the last fiscal year.

Exports of dog chews jumped by 77.87 percent to Rs1.49 billion during the review period. The country exported dog chews worth Rs4.81 billion in the last fiscal year.

Demand for Nepali dog chews has been growing in the United States, Canada, and other countries.

Fabric exports rose by 41.05 percent to Rs1.12 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year. Nepal shipped fabrics worth Rs3.6 billion in the last fiscal year.

Footwear exports increased by 32.17 percent to Rs1 billion in the first three months of the current fiscal year. Exports stood at Rs3.19 billion last year.

Nepal’s ginger exports increased by 38.03 percent to Rs249.36 million, with 3,474 tonnes shipped. The country exported ginger worth Rs1.50 billion in the last fiscal year, with shipments totalling 17,254 tonnes.

Exports of iron and steel products surged by 369.42 percent to Rs4.71 billion in the first quarter. Nepal exported iron and steel products worth Rs6.14 billion in the last fiscal year.

Nepal’s iron and steel exports have come under pressure following India's imposition of safeguard duties.

Shipments of jute and jute products rose by 39.91 percent to Rs3.85 billion during the review period. The country exported jute and jute products worth Rs10.78 billion in the last fiscal year.

India’s decision to increase anti-dumping duties on Nepali jute products has added to the pressure on the country's jute industry, particularly in eastern Nepal, where most of the country's jute mills are based.

According to a notification issued by India's Ministry of Finance on September 24, 2026, anti-dumping duties on hessian fabric, jute bags, and jute yarn and twine have been set at different rates depending on the product and manufacturer.

Shipments of handmade paper increased by 16 percent to Rs417.02 million during the first quarter. Nepal exported handmade paper worth Rs1.21 billion in the last fiscal year.

Readymade garment exports grew by 52.68 percent to Rs3.83 billion, with 5.85 million pieces shipped. The country exported 15.52 million pieces of readymade garments worth Rs9.30 billion in the last fiscal year.

Nepal’s tea exports rose by 48 percent to Rs1.64 billion, with 5,426 tonnes shipped. The country exported 13,303 tonnes of tea worth Rs3.97 billion in the last fiscal year.

Pashmina shipments grew by 29.11 percent to Rs3.32 billion in the first quarter of the current fiscal year. The country exported pashmina worth Rs3.76 billion in the last fiscal year.

Carpet exports rose by 37.64 percent to Rs2.44 billion during the first three months of the current fiscal year. Nepal exported carpets worth Rs10.38 billion in the last fiscal year.

Felt exports increased by 15.68 percent to Rs1.28 billion during the review period. The country exported felt products worth Rs5.97 billion in the last fiscal year.

Yarn shipments increased by 48.74 percent to Rs5 billion in the first quarter of the current fiscal year. The country exported yarn worth Rs15.66 billion in the last fiscal year.

Exports of pasta rose by 121.94 percent to Rs1.58 billion during the review period.

Vegetable exports grew by 20.71 percent to Rs191.48 million. Nepal exported 11,319 tonnes of vegetables during the period.

Spice shipments increased by 93.42 percent to Rs148.48 million, with 841 tonnes exported.

Meanwhile, exports of cement, lentils, medicinal herbs, and fruits declined during the review period.

title: Rebuilding Nepal’s Politics For Accountable Governance - The Rising Nepal
description: Rebuilding Nepal’s Politics For Accountable Governance  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
The ability of people to elect wise leaders capable of representation and performance in the delivery of public goods is the hallmark of representative democracy. But participatory democracies driven by the information revolution demand more—direct communication with leaders, recognition of their dignity and emotional satisfaction from political engagements. Nepali leaders, however, seem febrile. They have failed to transform their political parties from tools of agitation to completely electoral machines capable of socialization, articulation of public interests, communication and social transformation. They seem weak in synchronizing with public admin in crafting public policies and animating the hope of people. As a result, governance in Nepal is sub-optimal. It seems far less efficient to solve a range of problems. Lord Krishna reveals in the Mahabharata a harsh reality of politics: a nation having too many politicians ensures no peace.

Nepali political parties’ intelligence lies in keeping political sight going non-stop without being answerable to the peeved cadres and people. The underlying political culture of factional habits has set a pathology that is eating the very vitality and positive vibes that elevated their leadership. Institution building of Nepali parties is at an embryonic phase, though their history of formation is elongated. They appear weak in transforming their patrimonial political culture into a civic one and operating according to constitutional mandate, public opinion and democratic habit formation so that the living conditions of Nepalis are uplifted to a dignified level, people are enabled to exercise their autonomy in voting and initiatives and articulate their voice and visibility in the decisions. Non-implementable political promises of prosperity and skewed fulfilment of people’s rights have become a driver of conflict in Nepal and a source of political flux. The cadres and people are often leery of non-performing politicians. There are certain structural pitfalls in Nepali politics that need to be tackled to set coherence in the theory and practice of democracy and the integrity of its system, which people prized and leaders struggled for long.

Youth revolt

Compatibility between the constitution and public policies: One of the ironies of Nepal’s development is the social democratic goal of the constitution to create an egalitarian society and the adoption of neo-liberal policies that created a wide gap in public and private education, health, economy and communication, which spawned an unequal playing field and stoked the emotions of the left-out sections of society. A radical shift of political power from gerontocracy to youth following the youth revolt has twisted an imbalance in the representation of its demographics. The triumph of youth has side-lined other variables of non-Gen-Z generations, class, gender, region and people of lower economic brackets who are demanding justice. The democratic system cannot keep its balance if the sub-system of Gen-Z dominates the entire system. It is not difficult for Nepali parties to win elections. What is important is whether both the winners and losers follow the rules of the game and help each other in shaping national public policies beneficial to all Nepalis or engage in odious and self-protective politics. The legitimacy of elections turns fleeting if the regime fails to enlist the cooperation of many dissidents in governance.

Coherence between winning in elections and governing: The problems of governance in Nepal spring from political instability arising out of the inability of the government to manage various forms of defiant actors within constitutional rules of conduct and put a tab on their temptation to topple the government without allowing it to fulfil its tenure or demand for power sharing, even if popular mandate goes against them. The growing perception among leaders that being in power means enriching oneself, becoming powerful, and holding the position lifelong until death must be replaced with a service orientation to the people. The creeping public doubts about the credibility of the government to fulfil its tenure, stabilize the institutions of the state to create rule of law and service delivery and provide a sense of stability are validated by persistent historical patterns. Political instability in Nepal is also caused by short-lived coalitions, lack of contextual planning and administrative competency and integrity of governing institutions in matters of ethical and constitutional conduct. This is why even a government with a two-thirds majority, a simple majority, a coalition, or a minority-party government could not stabilize its authority and enhance output legitimacy to foster a sense of democratic development.

Harmony between accountability and public responsiveness: Almost all the perspective plans have failed to achieve the targeted goals, cut poverty and retain youths within the nation. No guarantee exists that the government realizes all sustainable development goals so that no Nepali is left behind. The Nepali constitution has embraced the right to information of people, aiming to make statecraft transparent and accountable. It is an antidote to corruption, abuse of authority and crime, as these vices eat the vitals of democratic governance. Nepal’s admin is overtly partisan, interested more in career enrichment than meritocratic public service and displays poor ability karya dakchhata and karya chhamata (competence) in impartial performance. Clientele orientation, loyalty to dominant actors and a loop of patronage hamper this.

Corruption is the personalization of public wealth. It has drained the public resources needed for investment in resilient infrastructure, utilities, education, health, adaptation to climate change and improving the standards of society by injecting the elements of modernity. Strong enforcement of the rule of law, powerful oversight by watchdog agencies, media, civil society and an independent courts and criminal justice system can mitigate the culture of impunity and remove the nation’s tag from the grey list. Ironically, each political change in Nepal is devoured by its own architects. This pattern recurs often, thus leaving politics in a state of incandescence, heated by the infinite passion of leadership for power and the paroxysm of emotion of people ready to jump on the street. One key problem of Nepal is that power brokers have tied the executive, judiciary, law-enforcing agencies and corporate sectors and shielded them from being caught for evil acts, thus eroding public trust in the institutions of governance, whether they can build sane order and mete out justice in an impartial manner.

Inclusive governance and marginalization: The diversity of Nepal’s geography, language, culture, religion, economy and education is not a problem in cooperation if shared interests among them are crystallized in public policies and actors of governance are adapted to common goals through socialization on the Directive Principles and Policies of the State. When governance is sought outside the prerogative of the constitution and the Nepali state, it creates disharmony among the space, economy and people and hits performance. Policy failure in Nepal originates from the lack of proper enforcement. The market and civil society compete for resources and authority while remaining lifeless when the political sphere is bogged down by a logjam and conflict of interests, while society is afflicted by inflation and human-induced and natural misfortunes. In Nepal, workers, isolated communities, youth and political orphans do not have apt channels to participate in decisions and build their stake in governance. The constitution is not the sole problem. It offers space for social inclusion, affirmative action, positive discrimination and proportional representation. The problem springs from the incapacity of leaders to translate them into institutional practices to hone better wisdom about the future. A productive economy of farms and industries can alleviate poverty, create jobs, retain youth, contribute to welfare and execute social transformation. Social movements and youth revolt are the outcome of deficits in intergenerational justice in governance. Governance entails the ordering structures and a guide to various institutions, actors and processes as per the constitutional frame of equity, integrity, transparency and accountability. The international regime is also an external stakeholder that has set up a governance unit in its field offices and, therefore, its aid alignment to national priorities is vital for national coherence.

Digitised sphere

Congruity between modern technology and system of oversight: The cognitive map of human beings has social and historical origins. What people think is largely determined by the type of offline ecology, society, economy and polity they live in, not only online. But social media, social scientists and leaders are alienated from the concept of reflective thought about visual context. The use of written language and speech by leadership is losing lustre. In the digitised sphere, language is overtaken by images, video, the internet, artificial intelligence, and algorithmic stuff. It is altering the landscape of contact in the entire nation and turning the legacy of Nepali political parties’ genesis anti-diluvium while stoking techno-fears in the setup of data centres for their social, energy and pollution costs to people’s lives relative to the profits to techno-feudal. In Nepal, the pervading use of digital and artificial intelligence outpaces oversight and power checks, thus shrivelling the compliance of the deep state and thieves with national laws. The nation is caught in a peril of eternal political stir and populism.

The display of melodramatic politics and connectivity without the diffusion of values of democracy, human rights, social justice and solidarity to Nepalis no longer sets social standards to keep governance on the right track. The manipulation of courts by free riders or middleman and their ability to bring executive, administrative and judicial bodies into a collusive web of power against public interests has eroded the integrity of governance in the delivery of public goods. Governance entails breaking this undemocratic web so that institutions and leaders ardently fulfil the rationale of politics of compassion rather than engage in many side jobs with no concern for public and national interests and improve the nation’s fortune.

(Former Reader at the Department of Political Science, TU, Dahal writes on political and social issues.)

title: Youth Uprising To Democratic Transformation - The Rising Nepal
description: Youth Uprising To Democratic Transformation  The Rising Nepal
publisher.title: The Rising Nepal
full_article:
When I read an article titled 'Yes, protest still works. Serbia Just proved it' written by Srdja Popovic , founder of the Centre for applied non-violent actions and shared online through Journal of Democracy, I noticed some parallels of Serbia’s political rebellion with the Gen-Z movement of Nepal. However, there appear to be some significant differences between the two cases. Nepal’s Gen-Z movement was characterized by the sudden burst of anger of young people onto the streets, in which at least five dozen people were killed and destruction of public and private assets was wrought on an enormous scale. But in Serbia, the nature and methodology of protest have been characteristically different. The recent political change in Serbia was not brought about through sudden and abrupt popular resistance. It was caused by an almost two-year-long, protracted, youth-led, non-violent resistance that culminated in the ouster of the Aleksandar Vucic-led government.

Civic engagement

However, it has sent shockwaves across Europe and re-anchored the Balkan political landscape. The long-standing regime of Aleksandar Vucic and his ruling Serbian Progressive Party (SNS) has collapsed. What began as a localized cry for justice following a devastating structural tragedy blossomed into a formidable, two-year anti-corruption crusade led by university students. Culminating in a decisive electoral victory in the recent parliamentary elections, this movement established that sustained youth civic engagement can dismantle even the most entrenched authoritarian structures.

The fall of Vucic’s government in Serbia, which ended fourteen years of dominant rule, offers an excellent instance of how generational disillusionment can transform into an unstoppable democratic engine. To understand the collapse of the Serbian regime, one must look back to November 1, 2024, when a tragedy struck the northern city of Novi Sad. The newly renovated concrete canopy of the Novi Sad railway station, a high-profile infrastructure project linked to foreign investment deals, collapsed, killing 16 people. For years, citizens had quietly tolerated infrastructure delays, opaque state contracts, and rising living costs. However, the deaths at Novi Sad served as a grim symbol of state negligence. It was not perceived merely as an accident, but as the fatal consequence of systemic corruption, corner-cutting, and institutional unaccountability.

Public anger was immediate, but while traditional opposition political parties struggled to mobilize a cohesive narrative, Serbia’s university students stepped forward. What began as localized vigils and campus sit-ins in Belgrade and Novi Sad rapidly evolved into a sophisticated, multi-phased movement, writes Popovic. Serbian youth, drawn primarily from Gen Z, brought a fresh tactical repertoire to civil resistance. Rather than relying solely on weekend rallies, the student coalition implemented decentralized blockades. Key transit hubs, major highway intersections, and university administration buildings were systematically shut down. These actions were characterized by non-violent discipline.

The student organizers coordinated garbage cleanups, set up study circles, and held prolonged, silent vigils honoring the Novi Sad victims, confronting state police with quiet dignity. Crucially, the student organizers avoided insular academic jargon. They framed their movement not around abstract political ideologies, but around universal values: safety, justice, rule of law, and a future free from corruption. By early 2025, the protests had expanded beyond major university hubs into over 400 towns and rural communities across Serbia. Teachers, industrial workers, transit employees, and pensioners joined forces with the youth, transforming a student initiative into a broad-based popular uprising. For years, the ruling party had relied on a reliable formula to maintain control: controlling mainstream media, marginalizing political opponents, and deploying state-backed intimidation tactics. When faced with the student movement, the government attempted to deploy these same tactics—only to find them ineffective.

When pro-government media attempted to brand the students as foreign agents or paid agitators, the youth leveraged digital platforms, social media live streams, and independent news outlets to counter the state narrative. Attempts to intimidate protesters with heavy-handed police responses or counter-protests backfired, drawing even larger crowds into the streets. The government’s legitimacy fractured further as high-level resignations failed to appease the public. The movement’s core demand remained unyielding: total accountability for corrupt governance and an immediate, transparent return to the ballot box. By mid-2026, amid persistent strikes and nationwide disruptions, the regime's political authority had unraveled, forcing early elections.

The defining achievement of the movement was its decision to transition from street activism to institutional participation. Recognizing that protests alone could not seal a political transformation, student leaders organized the "Student List"-an electoral coalition featuring young activists, academics, civil society leaders, and independent experts. In the parliamentary elections of October 25, 2026, turnout among young voters reached record highs. Voting defense networks organized by students guarded polling sites across the country, preventing electoral irregularities.

Political rebuilding

When the votes were counted, the victory was overwhelming. The ruling coalition lost its majority, and the Student List secured a historic mandate to lead the nation's political rebuilding. Aleksandar Vučić was forced to concede defeat, marking the end of an era defined by centralized power. The collapse of the Serbian government carries profound implications for Southern and Eastern Europe. The success of Serbia’s youth demonstrates that autocratic consolidation is not irreversible, providing a potential template for pro-democracy movements across Eastern Europe. The new parliamentary leadership has prioritized judicial independence, freedom of the press, and strict oversight of public infrastructure contracts—realigning Serbia’s trajectory toward European integration standards.

The post-election period has already seen a wave of detentions and formal investigations into long-standing corruption cases that were previously ignored by the state prosecutor. The fall of the Serbian government was neither an overnight event nor an accidental political turn. It was the direct result of a sustained, strategic campaign waged by a generation determined to claim its future. By converting grief into activism and street resistance into electoral victory, Serbia’s youth have rewritten their nation’s story.

(The author is presently associated with Policy Research Institute (PRI) as a senior research fellow. rijalmukti@gmail.com)

title: Mountaineering, as war waged by other means - Nepali Times
description: Mountaineering, as war waged by other means  Nepali Times
publisher.title: Nepali Times
full_article:
While writing his new book, mountaineering historian Edward Morgan calculated the number of climbers who had been above 8,000m prior to the French Annapurna expedition of 1950.

It turns out 35 climbers had been higher than 8,000m, and the most famous of them were mountaineers like George Mallory. Of those 35, 20 were Sherpa or Tibetan porters on Mt Everest, Kangchejunga, or Nanga Parbat, none used bottled oxygen, and all carried heavy loads.

“I think the achievement of these 20 porters should be better known,” says Morgan, whose book 'Chasing Mallory’s Dream: The Race Between Britain and Germany to Climb the Himalayan Peaks' chronicles some of the extreme sacrifices made by climbers from Nepal and Tibet in Himalayan mountaineering during the interregnum between the two World Wars.

Nepali and Tibetan porters who took loads up to Camp VI at 8,170m on Mt Everest in 1924.

Britain and Germany had just emerged bruised and battered after WWI, and barely 21 years later, were preparing to kill each other all over again in WWII. But even then, their climbers were sometimes working together and learning from each other in the Himalaya.

Despite the bad blood between Germany and Britain there was a spirit of camaraderie and mutual respect among young mountaineers of both countries — even if they were on opposite sides of the trenches in the war. It was only later as the Nazis rose to power that climbers started regarding each other as rivals, dividing even the German alpine community over support for the Nazis.

Even so, Morgan’s carefully researched book with valuable archival images also points to British and German climbers continuing to cooperate and exchange notes right up to 1938.

Newspapers in both countries extolled the successes of each other’s Himalayan expeditions and offered sympathy when disasters struck — like the 1934 and 1937 German Nanga Parbat expeditions, which together killed 26 climbers, nine of whom were from Nepal.

German climbers on Elburz during the war.

Morgan (pictured, left) writes about how right up to a year before Britain declared war on Germany, the British in India helped the Germans recover bodies buried on Nanga Parbat Camp IV the previous year by flying the team to Gilgit in a Royal Air Force plane.

TRENCH TO PEAK

At a dinner at the Himalayan Club in Calcutta in 1930, British surveyor Kenneth Mason raised a toast saying “there is room for all climbers for all nations” in the Himalaya. German expedition leader Paul Bauer replied that Mallory and Irvine who had perished on Mt Everest in 1924 “will always live in the memory of those who try to follow their footprint”.

And that seems to be where Morgan gets the title of the book about ‘chasing Mallory’s dream’. His cast of characters is long: Britons Frank Smythe, Geoffrey Bruce, Tom Longstaff, Noel Odell, Eric Shipton, Bill Tilman, Edward Norton, John Noel; and German climbers Willi Merl, Günter Oskar Dyhrenfurth and his wife Hettie, Eugen Allwein, Peter Aschenbrenner, Peter Aufschnaiter, Heinrich Harrer.

title: Nepal’s Stolen Gods Are Coming Home – Hindu Press International - Hinduism Today

KATHMANDU, NEPAL, July 1, 2026 (Hinduism Today): For centuries, Nepal’s temples, courtyards and villages housed sacred statues that were not regarded merely as artworks but worshiped as living Gods. After Nepal opened to international visitors in the 1950s, growing global interest in its sacred art was followed by widespread theft. Thousands of statues and other religious objects were removed from temples and communities and entered international museums, galleries, auction houses and private collections.

Efforts to recover the lost heritage have grown substantially. Since formal repatriation efforts began in the 1980s, 201 sacred objects have been returned to Nepal, while activists and organizations such as the National Heritage Recovery Campaign and Lost Arts of Nepal continue to identify objects overseas and document their provenance. A January 2026 cultural-property agreement between Nepal and the United States also strengthens efforts to intercept illegally trafficked antiquities and return them to their communities.

Lisbon (Portugal). The Nepali Embassy in Lisbon, Portugal has started mentioning the national calendar 'Nepal Sambat' along with Bikram Sambat and the Gregorian calendar in its official notice letter.

On the same occasion, Nemkul had demanded that Nepal Sambat be respected as a national identity and historical heritage, and its use should be prioritized in the official correspondence, notices, and administrative work of Nepali embassies abroad.

Furthermore, he had handed over a request letter to the chief guest Ambassador Prakashmani Poudel, requesting that the historical importance and use of Nepal Sambat be included in Nepal's educational curriculum.

Nemkul has expressed his heartfelt gratitude to the Nepali Embassy in Lisbon for addressing his demand by giving a place to Nepal Sambat in the official notice. Stakeholders have said that this step is not just about adding a date, but a very positive and welcome beginning to place Nepal's original history, identity, culture, and national pride in government work and official records.

ANTALYA, Nov 14: Nepal and the Republic of Korea have signed a cooperation framework agreement on climate change aimed at mobilizing carbon finance, reducing greenhouse gas emissions and strengthening climate cooperation between the two countries.

(adsbygoogle = window.adsbygoogle || []).push({});

The agreement, reached under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement, is expected to create opportunities for cooperation in carbon markets, climate-friendly investment, technology transfer, climate adaptation and sustainable development.

Under the agreement, Nepal and South Korea will develop projects to reduce greenhouse gas emissions and facilitate the transfer of internationally recognized emission reduction outcomes. This is expected to help mobilize international carbon finance and attract public and private investment in climate adaptation and mitigation.

Related story SHIFT for Our Planet: Youths urge authorities to make climate j...

Energy, transport, industry, buildings, waste management, agriculture and forestry have been identified as priority areas. Climate-friendly projects, expanded investment and the use of advanced technologies will be promoted in these sectors.

The agreement also provides for transparent accounting, monitoring, reporting and verification (MRV) of carbon emissions, along with adjustment mechanisms to prevent the double counting of emission reductions. These measures are expected to help maintain environmental integrity in carbon trading and support the implementation of international climate commitments.

The agreement is also expected to support Nepal’s Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), strengthen climate resilience and contribute to the country’s goal of achieving net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2045.

A joint committee comprising government representatives from both countries will be formed to monitor implementation, approve joint action plans and oversee cooperation activities.

The Nepali government expressed confidence that the partnership would help mobilize climate finance, promote technology transfer and strengthen capacity building at a time when Nepal is facing increasing risks of floods and landslides and growing threats to mountainous regions due to climate change.

The agreement was signed by Dr Maheshwor Dhakal, joint secretary and focal person for the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change, on behalf of the Government of Nepal, and Jongho Kyun, ambassador for climate change and deputy minister of foreign affairs, on behalf of the Government of South Korea.

full_article:
Kathmandu. Nepal Telecommunications Company Limited (Nepal Telecom) has seen a significant improvement in its net profit in the first quarter of the current fiscal year 2083/84.

According to the company's unaudited financial statement for the first quarter of the current fiscal year, published until the end of Ashwin, net profit has increased by 37.35 percent to Rs 1.82 billion and 1 million. In the same period of the last fiscal year, the company's net profit was Rs 1.32 billion and 51 million.

Based on this, the company's net profit has increased by Rs 494.9 million during the review period. Along with this, the company's annualized Earnings Per Share (EPS) has been fixed at Rs 40.45.

During the review period, the company's total operating income reached Rs 8.67 billion and 82 million. This amount is Rs 1.26 million or 0.01 percent higher than the total operating income of Rs 8.67 billion and 95 million in the same period of the last fiscal year.

Similarly, in the first three months of the current fiscal year, the company's total income reached Rs 9.47 billion and 76 million. Compared to Rs 9.47 billion and 10 million in the same period of the last fiscal year, the total income has increased by Rs 6.64 million or 0.07 percent, the statement mentions.

According to the financial statement, profit before interest, tax, depreciation, and amortization (EBITDA) has decreased by 6.13 percent. EBITDA, which was Rs 4.75 billion and 4 million in the first quarter of last year, has decreased by Rs 291.4 million this year to Rs 4.45 billion and 90 million.

Despite this, the company's profit before tax has increased by 3.65 percent. Telecom has stated that the profit before tax, which was Rs 2.88 billion and 21 million last year, has increased by Rs 105.2 million to Rs 2.98 billion and 74 million.

During the first quarter, natural disasters adversely affected Telecom's service sales and revenue. On Bhadra 10, Telecom provided free data and voice services for 17 days to affected service recipients due to the devastating flood and landslide in the Bhotekoshi area of Rasuwa district.

The company mentioned that the telecommunication service was disrupted in the affected areas due to the natural disaster, and business activities were also hampered. Similarly, the service was negatively impacted due to the flood in the Budhigandaki River on Ashwin 25. The company stated that the free service and operational disruptions affected revenue from service sales.

Despite the adversities, the increase in GSM service operating revenue due to affordable prices and the growing use of large mobile data packages has helped increase operating revenue, the statement mentions. During this period, operating revenue for GSM services increased by Rs 1.016 million and for FTTH services by Rs 44 million.

Similarly, although employee expenses increased due to salary scale adjustments, the company's total expenses decreased by 5.90 percent, or Rs 481.2 million, due to a reduction in depreciation expenses and impairment reversal.

Telecom has stated that it is also providing services in remote locations that are costly and have low returns. Regarding the review period, the statement says, 'The work of expanding services and improving quality in remote and inaccessible areas with high costs and low returns has been prioritized.'

The company has clarified that it is continuing the process of service improvement by extending telecommunication access to remote settlements.
